chapters.title: Sampling frames, stratification and allocation

concepts.title: Define the target and frame
concepts.text: The target population is the group about which an inference is intended. A sampling frame lists units that can actually be selected. Undercoverage, duplicates and nonresponse can bias results even when the nominal sample size is large. A census can also suffer measurement and coverage errors.

concepts.title: Distinguish selection mechanisms
concepts.text: In simple random sampling without replacement, each subset of size n has equal probability. Stratified sampling selects within strata; cluster sampling selects groups. Systematic sampling uses an interval and random start, but periodic ordering can distort the sample. Convenience and judgment selection do not provide known inclusion probabilities.

concepts.title: Allocate and assess precision
concepts.text: Proportional allocation uses nh=nNh/N. Under equal unit costs and known within-stratum standard deviations, Neyman allocation uses nh proportional to NhSh. Sampling error concerns random selection variability; nonsampling error includes mismeasurement, coverage and processing. State replacement and independence assumptions before calculating a standard error.

example.problem: Two strata have populations 600 and 400. Allocate a sample of 50 proportionally.

chapters.mistake: A bigger convenience sample does not automatically remove selection bias.

chapters.title: Grouped distributions, quantiles and graphical summaries

concepts.title: Make the classes unambiguous
concepts.text: Use mutually exclusive, exhaustive classes and state boundary conventions. Relative frequency equals class frequency divided by total frequency. Cumulative frequency totals the observations up to a boundary. In a histogram with unequal widths, frequency corresponds to area; height must use frequency density.

concepts.title: Estimate from grouped data
concepts.text: A grouped mean uses class midpoints and weights: Σfimi/Σfi. This is an estimate unless the midpoint represents each observation. For a continuous grouped median, the usual interpolation is L+[(N/2−F)/f]h, where F precedes the median class. It assumes suitable within-class interpolation.

concepts.title: Interpret partitions and modes
concepts.text: Quartiles and percentiles partition an ordered distribution. Finite-sample conventions can differ; specify the one used. For the grouped mode, the standard interpolation uses the modal frequency and adjacent frequencies; it is not just the modal class midpoint. A frequency polygon joins midpoint-frequency positions and should retain meaningful axis scales.

example.problem: Classes 0–10 and 10–20 have frequencies 2 and 6. Estimate the mean from midpoints.

chapters.mistake: Do not average class midpoints without weighting their frequencies.

chapters.title: Dispersion, transformations and coefficients

concepts.title: Specify the dispersion measure
concepts.text: Range uses extreme values and is sensitive to outliers. Interquartile range is Q3−Q1; quartile deviation is half that. Mean absolute deviation and standard deviation measure different deviations. Population variance divides squared deviations by N, whereas the usual unbiased sample variance divides by n−1.

concepts.title: Transform correctly
concepts.text: Adding a constant changes location but leaves variance unchanged. Multiplying observations by b multiplies variance by b² and standard deviation by |b|. For independent sums, variances add; without independence include covariance terms. The standard deviation has the original measurement units, while variance has squared units.

concepts.title: Use relative spread appropriately
concepts.text: Coefficient of variation is 100 s/mean in a suitable ratio-scale setting with a meaningful nonzero mean. It can be misleading near zero or for arbitrary temperature origins. Do not compare variance numerically across incompatible units without converting them first.

example.problem: X has mean 10 and standard deviation 3. For Y=2X+5 find mean, standard deviation and variance.

chapters.mistake: Variance is multiplied by b², not by b.

chapters.title: Moments, skewness and kurtosis

concepts.title: Keep raw and central moments distinct
concepts.text: The kth raw moment is E[X^k]; the kth central moment is E[(X−μ)^k]. The first raw moment is the mean and the first central moment is zero. The second central moment is variance. Expand the algebra before substituting, especially when converting raw moments to central moments.

concepts.title: Standardise shape with conditions
concepts.text: For positive variance, moment skewness is μ3/σ³ and kurtosis is μ4/σ⁴. Excess kurtosis subtracts 3; the convention must be named. Positive skew usually means a longer right tail, but shortcut mean-median-mode orderings are not universal characterisations of every possible distribution.

concepts.title: Use transformation invariance
concepts.text: A positive scale and a location shift do not change standardised moment shape. A negative scale reverses the sign of skewness but leaves kurtosis unchanged. A constant distribution has zero variance, so standardised skewness/kurtosis are undefined rather than automatically zero.

example.problem: For X equally likely to be −1 or 1, calculate variance, moment skewness and kurtosis.
steps: The third central moment is zero by symmetry.
E[X⁴]=1, so kurtosis=1 and excess kurtosis=−2.

recall: Keep raw and central moments distinct
chapters.mistake: Kurtosis and excess kurtosis differ by 3.

chapters.title: Pearson, rank and partial correlation

concepts.title: Calculate a standardised association
concepts.text: Pearson r=Cov(X, Y)/(σxσy) when both standard deviations are positive. It measures linear association and is bounded by −1 and 1. A nonlinear deterministic relation can still have r=0. Adding constants does not affect r; multiplying one variable by a negative factor reverses its sign.

concepts.title: Rank consistently
concepts.text: For n pairs without ties, Spearman rho=1−6Σd²/[n(n²−1)]. Ties require appropriate ranks and a suitable correlation calculation rather than blind use of the no-tie shortcut. Correlation of attributes deals with categorical association and needs the relevant contingency counts.

concepts.title: Control one variable algebraically
concepts.text: For three variables, partial r 12.3=(r 12−r 13 r 23)/√[(1−r 13²)(1−r 23²)] when the denominator is nonzero. Partial association is conditional on the measured variables and model; it does not prove causation or remove bias from unmeasured confounding.

example.problem: Without rank ties, n=4 and Σd²=4. Find Spearman correlation.

chapters.mistake: Zero Pearson correlation does not imply general independence.

chapters.title: Regression lines, residuals and least squares

concepts.title: Fit the stated response
concepts.text: In simple regression Y=a+bX with an intercept, b=Sxy/Sxx=r sy/sx and a=ybar−b xbar. The fitted line passes through the sample means. Minimising vertical residual squares for Y-on-X differs from predicting X from Y; in general the slopes are not reciprocals.

concepts.title: Inspect residual properties
concepts.text: With an estimated intercept, ordinary least-squares residuals sum to zero. This algebra does not prove model suitability. Look for curvature, changing spread and influential observations. In simple regression with an intercept, R²=r²; this identity need not apply to every model specification.

concepts.title: Separate association and uncertainty
concepts.text: A coefficient measures conditional association within the fitted model. Multiple regression holds included regressors constant algebraically; omitted variables and simultaneity can still bias causal interpretation. Prediction intervals for a new observation include individual noise in addition to uncertainty about the conditional mean.

example.problem: Given xbar=4, ybar=10, r=0.5, sx=2, sy=6, find the Y-on-X line and fitted value at X=6.

chapters.mistake: Do not reverse a regression line by simply taking a reciprocal slope.

chapters.title: Counting, conditional probability and Bayes updating

concepts.title: Count equiprobable outcomes only when justified
concepts.text: For equally likely finite outcomes, probability is favourable count divided by total count. Addition uses P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B). For sequences multiply appropriate conditional probabilities, not marginal probabilities unless independence is justified.

concepts.title: Condition on the information given
concepts.text: Conditioning changes the reference population to the given event. Drawing without replacement generally changes subsequent probabilities. Independence and mutual exclusivity are different properties; two disjoint events with positive probabilities cannot be independent.

concepts.title: Update using the total evidence
concepts.text: For an exhaustive disjoint partition Bi, P(Bi|A)=P(A|Bi)P(Bi)/ΣjP(A|Bj)P(Bj). Low base rates can keep posterior probability modest even with an apparently informative signal. Always compute the denominator across all possible generating groups.

example.problem: Boxes A and B are chosen with equal probability. Red probabilities are 0.8 in A and 0.2 in B. Given red, find P(A|red).

recall: Count equiprobable outcomes only when justified
chapters.mistake: P(A|B) and P(B|A) are not interchangeable.

chapters.title: Discrete distributions and joint random variables

concepts.title: Validate and marginalise
concepts.text: A discrete joint probability table must have nonnegative entries summing to one. Marginalise by summing rows or columns. Calculate conditional probabilities by dividing the joint probability by the relevant positive marginal. Joint independence requires every joint cell to equal the product of its marginals.

concepts.title: Use the binomial model deliberately
concepts.text: For n independent trials with common success probability p, P(X=k)=C(n, k)p^k(1−p)^(n−k), E[X]=np and Var(X)=np(1−p). Sampling without replacement from a finite population generally uses a hypergeometric model rather than exact binomial independence.

concepts.title: Read Poisson and covariance correctly
concepts.text: A Poisson count with parameter λ has mass exp(−λ)λ^k/k!, mean λ and variance λ. For a transformed random variable E[aX+b]=aE[X]+b. Var(X+Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y)+2Cov(X, Y); the covariance term cannot be dropped merely because both variables are random.

example.problem: X is binomial with n=3, p=1/2. Calculate P(X=2).
steps: Choose the two successes in C(3,2)=3 ways.

chapters.mistake: Equal marginal distributions do not imply independence.

chapters.title: Continuous distributions and standardisation

concepts.title: Separate density from probability
concepts.text: A continuous density is nonnegative and integrates to one. Probability on an interval is an integral, not the density value at one point. For a continuous distribution, a single exact value has probability zero even when its density is positive. A cumulative distribution gives P(X≤x).

concepts.title: Standardise a normal variable
concepts.text: For X normal with mean μ and positive SD σ, Z=(X−μ)/σ is standard normal. Its symmetry gives P(Z>0)=1/2. A normal mean and variance do not themselves describe arbitrary non-normal distributions, so normal-tail calculations require the model assumption.

concepts.title: Use rate and scale consistently
concepts.text: For an exponential waiting time with rate λ>0, survival is exp(−λt), mean 1/λ and variance 1/λ². Its memorylessness is a distributional property, not true of every waiting time. Uniform(a, b) has mean (a+b)/2 and variance (b−a)²/12.

example.problem: X is normal with mean 50 and SD 5. Standardise X=60 and identify the symmetric central interval corresponding to |Z|≤2.

chapters.mistake: Variance 25 means SD 5, not SD 25.

chapters.title: Estimators, likelihood and confidence intervals

concepts.title: Name the repeated-sampling property
concepts.text: An estimator is unbiased if its expectation equals the target parameter. Mean squared error equals variance plus squared bias. Consistency concerns convergence as n grows; it is not the same as unbiasedness for each finite n. Standard error is the sampling SD of an estimator, not the raw-data SD.

concepts.title: Construct an estimator from the model
concepts.text: Method of moments equates sample moments to model moments. Maximum likelihood maximises the probability/density of the observed data as a function of permitted parameters. Boundary constraints matter: an interior derivative equation may miss the maximum. Least squares minimises a sum of squared residuals and coincides with MLE only under appropriate error models.

concepts.title: Build an interval with its assumptions
concepts.text: For an independent normal sample with known σ, the mean interval is xbar±z σ/√n. If σ is unknown and normal sampling assumptions hold, use s and a t critical value with n−1 degrees of freedom. Confidence refers to the long-run coverage procedure. Narrowing the margin generally needs a larger sample or a lower confidence level.

example.problem: A normal population has known SD 6. With n=36 and sample mean 25, use z=1.96 for a 95% mean interval.

recall: Construct an estimator from the model
Build an interval with its assumptions
chapters.mistake: A realised frequentist interval is not a posterior distribution over μ.

chapters.title: Hypothesis tests, chi-square, F and ANOVA

concepts.title: Frame a decision under a null
concepts.text: State H0, the alternative, significance level, test statistic and its null distribution. A p-value measures how extreme the statistic is under H0; it is not P(H0 is true). Type I error is rejection of a true null; Type II error is failing to reject a false null. Statistical significance does not measure practical effect size.

concepts.title: Match statistic to assumptions
concepts.text: A normal-mean z statistic uses known σ; a one-sample t uses estimated s under its assumptions. Chi-square goodness-of-fit sums (observed−expected)²/expected and adjusts degrees of freedom for constraints and fitted parameters. A contingency independence test uses (rows−1)(columns−1) degrees of freedom. A variance-ratio F test needs suitable independent normal samples.

concepts.title: Decompose variation in ANOVA
concepts.text: One-way ANOVA partitions total sum of squares into between-group and within-group components. F=MSbetween/MSwithin with degrees k−1 and N−k. A significant result says not all means are equal, not that every pair differs. Two-way ANOVA adds another factor; interaction assessment depends on replication and design.

example.problem: Three groups contain 15 observations in total. Between-group SS=24 and within-group SS=36. Find the one-way ANOVA F statistic.

recall: Frame a decision under a null
chapters.mistake: Do not claim every group pair differs after one omnibus test.

chapters.title: Time-series components and weighted index numbers

concepts.title: Choose a time model
concepts.text: An additive decomposition writes observation=trend+seasonal+other components; a multiplicative decomposition uses products and is appropriate when variation scales with the level. Moving averages smooth but can conceal turning points. Seasonal comparison must use a defined periodicity and enough observations.

concepts.title: Define the weighted index
concepts.text: Laspeyres price index is 100Σp 1 q 0/Σp 0 q 0; Paasche uses q 1 in both sums. Fisher is the geometric mean of those two indices. A simple average of relatives need not equal a weighted aggregate. State whether the index concerns prices, quantities or values.

concepts.title: Rebase and splice carefully
concepts.text: If compatible index values are 150 and 120 on an old base, rebasing the first relative to the second gives 125. Linking two series requires an overlap and compatible coverage; a changed basket or classification may need more than rescaling. Cost-of-living interpretation depends on its consumption framework and weights.

example.problem: Two goods have p 0=(2,4), p 1=(3,6), q 0=(10,5). Calculate the Laspeyres price index.
steps: Current prices on the base basket cost 3×10+6×5=60.
example.answer: 150, a 50% increase for that base basket.

chapters.mistake: An index of 150 is a level, not 150% growth.

chapters.title: Double entry, accruals and rectification

concepts.title: Separate the entity and the owner
concepts.text: Business records distinguish the entity from its owner. Capital introduced increases cash/assets and equity; drawings reduce equity rather than operating profit as a business expense. Debit and credit describe account sides, not universally increases and decreases. Use Assets=Liabilities+Equity to check a transaction.

concepts.title: Follow accrual timing
concepts.text: Record expenses when incurred and revenue when earned under the stated recognition assumptions. An unpaid current expense produces an expense and liability; a prepaid future expense is initially an asset. Consistency aids comparison but does not require continuing an erroneous policy. Prudence does not justify deliberate hidden reserves or arbitrary understatement.

concepts.title: Find the error before correcting
concepts.text: Post journal entries to ledger accounts, balance them and prepare the trial balance. Complete omission, compensating errors and wrong-account entries can preserve equality. A suspense account can temporarily reconcile a one-sided difference, but must be cleared through explained correcting entries rather than treated as income.

example.problem: An owner introduces ₹30,000 cash, then the business incurs ₹4,000 rent unpaid. State assets, liabilities and equity.
steps: Cash asset increases to ₹30,000 and capital to ₹30,000.
Accrued rent adds an expense and liability of ₹4,000.

recall: Separate the entity and the owner
chapters.mistake: Drawings and business expenses have different effects on profit.

chapters.title: Cash books, bank balances and reconciliation signs

concepts.title: Choose one balance convention
concepts.text: From the business perspective, a positive bank asset is a debit cash-book balance; an overdraft is negative in a signed numerical representation. A bank statement uses the bank perspective, so the debit/credit wording reverses. Translate the words into signed balances before applying reconciling items.

concepts.title: Distinguish timing from missing entries
concepts.text: An issued cheque not yet presented has already reduced the cash book but not the statement balance. A deposit not yet credited has already increased the cash book but not the statement. Bank charges and direct debits missing from the cash book require updating it; they should not be counted a second time as timing items.

concepts.title: Reconcile without double counting
concepts.text: Start from an explicitly named adjusted balance and show each difference once. From a positive adjusted cash-book asset balance, add unpresented issued cheques and subtract uncredited deposits to reach the statement balance. Signed arithmetic can also handle overdrafts when the starting convention is consistent.

example.problem: Adjusted cash-book balance is +₹8,000. Issued cheques of ₹2,000 are unpresented; deposits of ₹1,500 are not credited. Find the statement balance.
steps: Add 2,000 because the statement has not yet recorded that payment.
Subtract 1,500 because the statement has not yet recorded that deposit.

chapters.mistake: A missing bank charge first adjusts the cash book; do not subtract it twice.

chapters.title: Bills of exchange and ledger control accounts

concepts.title: Identify each party
concepts.text: The drawer issues the payment order, the drawee is directed to pay and the payee receives the payment. Acceptance creates the accepted bill obligation under the stated arrangement. Distinguish a bill receivable held as an asset from a bill payable representing a liability. The legal validity and maturity rules require applicable law and instrument terms.

concepts.title: Track the bill lifecycle
concepts.text: A holder may retain, endorse, discount or send a bill for collection. In a simple discounting problem, bank discount=face value×annual rate×unexpired time under the stated day-count convention. Dishonour restores the relevant debtor obligation; recoverable noting charges can be added when the problem specifies them.

concepts.title: Use control totals for a ledger
concepts.text: A receivables control account summarises opening debtors, credit sales, receipts, returns, bad debts and closing debtors. Self-balancing ledger systems add adjustment accounts so separate ledgers can balance. Control-account agreement is useful but does not prove every individual posting or authorisation is correct.

example.problem: A ₹12,000 bill is discounted for 3 months at an assumed simple annual discount rate of 8%, with no fees. Find proceeds.

recall: Use control totals for a ledger
chapters.mistake: Use the unexpired term and specified day count; do not invent grace-day treatment.

chapters.title: Trading, manufacturing and not-for-profit statements

concepts.title: Build the cost flow
concepts.text: For a simple periodic inventory model, goods available=opening inventory+net purchases+direct acquisition costs; subtract closing inventory to get cost of goods sold. Gross profit=net sales−cost of goods sold. Manufacturing cost can include raw materials consumed, direct labour and factory overhead with work-in-progress adjustments.

concepts.title: Separate gross and net performance
concepts.text: Operating expenses and other income/expenses bridge gross profit to net profit under the stated classification. A balance sheet reports resources and obligations at a date, not the period flow of sales. Capital and revenue items must be identified by substance; the fact that cash was paid does not decide their classification.

concepts.title: Adjust a nonprofit cash summary
concepts.text: Receipts and payments record cash movements regardless of the related period. Income and expenditure reports accrual performance: adjust subscriptions for opening/closing outstanding and advance balances. Capital receipts, asset purchases and noncash depreciation require separate treatment rather than automatic inclusion as current income or expense.

example.problem: Net sales 90,000, opening inventory 10,000, purchases 50,000, closing inventory 12,000 and operating expenses 8,000 are given. Find gross and net profit.

chapters.mistake: A cash receipt may belong to a future period or be capital in nature.

chapters.title: Asset cost allocation, inventory and disposal

concepts.title: Identify depreciable cost and method
concepts.text: Straight-line depreciation allocates cost less residual value over useful life. A reducing-balance method applies a rate to the opening carrying amount. Initial costs necessary to bring an asset to working condition can form part of cost under the stated framework. Routine servicing and improvements must be distinguished.

concepts.title: Keep inventory quantities and valuation separate
concepts.text: In a periodic cost-flow model, FIFO assigns the earliest costs to issues first; a weighted average uses a specified averaging convention. Inventory units reconcile opening+receipts−issues=closing. A change in selling price is not itself a change in historical acquisition cost; valuation and impairment require the applicable framework.

concepts.title: Calculate a disposal result
concepts.text: Before disposal, update depreciation to the disposal date using the problem assumptions. Carrying amount=cost−accumulated depreciation−relevant impairments. Disposal gain/loss is net proceeds minus that carrying amount. The selling price does not retroactively replace original asset cost.

example.problem: An asset costs 40,000, residual value 4,000, useful life 6 years. It is sold after two full years for 25,000 with no fees. Find the disposal result.

recall: Keep inventory quantities and valuation separate
chapters.mistake: A disposal loss uses carrying amount, not original cost alone.

chapters.title: Consumer equilibrium, demand and elasticity

concepts.title: Separate a curve from a shift
concepts.text: An own-price demand curve holds income, preferences and relevant other prices fixed. A change in own price causes movement along the curve; another determinant can shift it. Normal and inferior goods are classified by income response, not by whether their quality is subjectively liked.

concepts.title: State the elasticity convention
concepts.text: Point price elasticity is (dQ/dP)(P/Q). An initial-value percentage and midpoint arc calculation can differ for the same finite change. Own-price elasticity is usually negative under ordinary downward-sloping demand; absolute value is often used for labels. Income and cross-price elasticities concern different changing variables.

concepts.title: Read equilibrium conditions with constraints
concepts.text: In an interior indifference-curve optimum under standard differentiability and convexity assumptions, MRS equals the price ratio and the budget is exhausted for nonsatiated preferences. Corner solutions require separate analysis. In a cardinal utility framework, compare marginal utility per rupee; do not mix a total-utility number with marginal utility.

example.problem: Demand is Q=100−2P. At P=20, calculate point own-price elasticity.

recall: Separate a curve from a shift
chapters.mistake: Elasticity is a proportional response, not just the demand-curve slope.

chapters.title: Production, costs and profit maximisation

concepts.title: Distinguish horizons and marginal concepts
concepts.text: Short-run production varies some inputs while at least one is fixed. Marginal product is extra output from an extra unit of the varying input. Diminishing marginal product can occur while total output still rises. Long-run returns to scale vary all inputs proportionally and are not the same concept.

concepts.title: Build cost identities
concepts.text: TC=TFC+TVC; average cost TC/Q for Q>0; marginal cost is the change in total cost per output change. Average fixed cost falls as positive output grows. A sunk cost is already incurred and irrecoverable under the stated decision, while opportunity cost is the value of the best forgone alternative.

concepts.title: Use marginal conditions with checks
concepts.text: An interior differentiable profit optimum satisfies MR=MC, with appropriate second-order and boundary checks. For a price taker MR equals the given market price. The short-run shutdown decision compares revenue with avoidable variable costs, while long-run exit also considers the full cost position.

example.problem: Total cost is TC=100+5Q+Q². At Q=10 find AC and marginal cost.

chapters.mistake: A zero derivative alone does not establish a global maximum.

chapters.title: Market structures, equilibrium and welfare

concepts.title: Solve market clearing under a model
concepts.text: A competitive partial-equilibrium model sets quantity demanded equal to quantity supplied, under its assumptions. A shortage at a controlled price means demand exceeds supply at that price; it does not by itself describe the allocation rule or the entire long-run adjustment.

concepts.title: Compare market structures
concepts.text: An ideal competitive firm takes price as given. A monopoly faces the market demand curve, with marginal revenue generally below price for downward-sloping demand. Monopolistic competition includes differentiation and entry; oligopoly involves strategic interdependence among a small number of important firms. Merely counting shops does not establish all assumptions.

concepts.title: Keep welfare tools conditional
concepts.text: Consumer surplus measures willingness to pay above payment in the standard demand-based model; producer surplus is not identical to accounting profit with fixed costs. Taxes can create a wedge between buyer and seller prices. The statutory payer and economic incidence can differ depending on elasticities and market conditions.

example.problem: Demand Qd=100−P and supply Qs=20+P. Find the model equilibrium.

recall: Solve market clearing under a model
chapters.mistake: Monopoly profit maximisation uses MR, not price alone, against MC.

chapters.title: National income, real output and circular flows

concepts.title: Choose the boundary and period
concepts.text: Domestic measures concern production within an economic territory; national measures incorporate relevant net primary income across residents and nonresidents. Production is a flow over a period. Intermediate inputs are subtracted in value added to prevent double counting; resale of an existing asset is not the same as producing it again.

concepts.title: Distinguish valuation and depreciation
concepts.text: Under the stated accounting conventions, gross minus consumption of fixed capital gives net. Market-price GDP relates to basic-price GVA through taxes less subsidies on products. Define valuation before mixing aggregates. Wages, profits and other primary income categories enter the income approach under a consistent accounting system.

concepts.title: Separate nominal and real changes
concepts.text: Nominal output uses current prices; real output uses a consistent price/volume framework. A simple GDP deflator is nominal/real×100 with matched coverage. In the expenditure identity, exports are added and imports subtracted because imported expenditure is included elsewhere; this subtraction does not mean imports have no consumer value.

example.problem: Consumption=200, investment=70, government final spending=50, exports=30 and imports=40. Find expenditure GDP in this simplified model.

chapters.mistake: Stocks of wealth and flows of current production are different quantities.

chapters.title: Money, banking, budgets and fiscal arithmetic

concepts.title: Describe functions rather than current rates
concepts.text: Money serves as a medium of exchange, unit of account and store of value within its institutional setting. Commercial banks accept deposits and extend credit subject to constraints. RBI monetary-policy tools and regulatory instruments have distinct mechanisms; a textbook example with an assumed rate is not a statement of today’s rate.

concepts.title: Use the multiplier as a simplified model
concepts.text: In a very simple reserve-only deposit model without currency leakage, an assumed reserve ratio r gives a theoretical deposit multiplier 1/r. Real money/credit creation is constrained by more factors, including capital, demand, liquidity and behaviour. Do not treat the simple multiplier as a mechanical forecast for an actual bank system.

concepts.title: Keep budget balances distinct
concepts.text: Revenue deficit=revenue expenditure−revenue receipts. Fiscal deficit=total expenditure−receipts excluding borrowings under the stated classification. Primary deficit=fiscal deficit−interest payments. Borrowing finances a deficit; it is not included as a nondebt receipt to make the deficit disappear. Stock debt and annual deficit are different.

example.problem: Total expenditure is 1000, revenue receipts 650 and nondebt capital receipts 100. Interest payments are 80. Calculate fiscal and primary deficits.

recall: Describe functions rather than current rates
Use the multiplier as a simplified model
chapters.mistake: These are illustrative figures, not current Indian budget values.

chapters.title: Indian development, poverty and infrastructure indicators

concepts.title: Compare shares on the same basis
concepts.text: Primary activities use natural resources, secondary activities transform materials and tertiary activities supply services. Classification boundaries follow the relevant statistical system. Employment shares and value-added shares answer different questions; a sector can employ many people without producing the same proportion of total measured value added.

concepts.title: Name the denominator and reference period
concepts.text: Unemployment rate=unemployed/labour force, not unemployed/total population. Labour-force participation compares labour force with the defined reference population; worker-population ratio compares employed people with it. Status definitions and reference periods matter. Poverty measures depend on a stated threshold and method; do not combine incomparable series.

concepts.title: Interpret development with several indicators
concepts.text: Income growth alone does not fully describe health, education, distribution, environment or access to infrastructure. A demographic dividend is an opportunity that depends on skills, employment and participation, not an automatic result of a larger working-age share. Use dated official statistics for actual current values rather than undated coaching summaries.

example.problem: In an illustrative reference population of 1000, the labour force is 600 and employed people number 540. Find unemployment rate, LFPR and worker-population ratio.

recall: Compare shares on the same basis
Name the denominator and reference period
chapters.mistake: Changing the denominator can create a false trend.

chapters.title: Public audit, Finance Commission and accountable digital services

concepts.title: Separate audit from executive spending
concepts.text: Public audit examines accounts and relevant use of public resources within its constitutional/statutory remit. The CAG is not the executive authority making every expenditure decision. Article 148 concerns the CAG institution; Article 280 provides for the Finance Commission. Use the current official constitutional text for wording, exceptions and amendments.

concepts.title: Understand intergovernmental recommendations
concepts.text: The Finance Commission recommends specified fiscal arrangements concerning Union-state and related transfers under its constitutional mandate. It is not a commercial bank or the central bank’s monetary policy committee. Distinguish a recommendation, a government decision, a budget provision and an actual measured outcome.

concepts.title: Evaluate digital governance as a service
concepts.text: Digitisation should support accountable processes, accessibility, authentication, privacy and grievance handling. Publishing excessive personal data is not automatically transparency. An audit trail helps trace authorised changes, while role-based access limits operations to their legitimate users. A public portal needs offline/assisted routes where exclusion is a concern.

example.problem: A digital grant portal lets every employee edit all applications without an audit trail. Identify two process controls.
steps: Define roles and restrict each role to necessary operations.
Record who changed what and when in an accountable audit trail.
Provide review and correction procedures rather than silently overwriting records.
example.answer: Role-based access and auditable change records.

recall: Evaluate digital governance as a service
chapters.mistake: A digital interface does not itself prove accountable administration.

chapters.title: External accounts, reforms and policy comparisons

concepts.title: Distinguish the accounts
concepts.text: The current account records goods, services and primary/secondary income categories under the relevant balance-of-payments framework. Financial transactions have their own classification; do not relabel every external inflow as export revenue. Accounting balances include offsetting entries and adjustment items, so a current-account deficit is not a claim that the entire record cannot balance.

concepts.title: State an exchange-rate convention
concepts.text: If rupees per dollar rise, more rupees are required for one dollar: the rupee depreciates against the dollar under that quotation. Effects on domestic-currency import cost depend on the foreign price, quantities, contracts and pass-through. An exchange-rate change alone does not guarantee an improvement in the trade balance.

concepts.title: Separate reforms, frameworks and outcomes
concepts.text: The 1991 reform discussion includes liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation, but these are distinct policy dimensions. Disinvestment reduces government ownership; it does not in every case transfer control. FRBM is a fiscal-responsibility/budget-management framework; current statutory targets and amendments must be checked in current official documents. Historical policy names are not evidence for today’s target values.

example.problem: An import costs $200. Compare rupee cost at ₹80/$ and ₹85/$, holding the dollar price fixed.
steps: The rupee cost rises ₹1,000; the rupee has depreciated under this quote.
example.answer: ₹16,000 to ₹17,000, with the stated fixed foreign price.

chapters.mistake: Always name which currency is in the numerator.

chapters.title: Ancient India: cities, states and historical evidence

concepts.title: Build separate evidence timelines
concepts.text: Archaeology examines material remains such as settlements, tools, pottery and burials. Inscriptions and coins supply different information from later literary traditions. A source must be located in time and context before using it to support a claim. Absence of one kind of evidence is not automatically proof that an activity never occurred.

concepts.title: Connect settlements and political change
concepts.text: Harappan urban settlements are associated with planned streets, drainage and craft/trade evidence; do not assign every site identical features. Early historic states and the Mauryan empire belong to a later setting. Ashoka belongs to the Mauryan dynasty, while the Gupta period is later; similar royal names across dynasties must not be conflated.

concepts.title: Classify a question before recalling
concepts.text: Separate a site-feature question from a ruler-dynasty match and a chronology question. For belief traditions, distinguish teachings, texts, communities and later patronage. Build a two-column source/evidence note and verify the specific association in the linked history material. These essentials are a starting framework, not a substitute for a complete ancient-history textbook.

example.problem: A note uses a much later story as direct proof of the exact layout of an ancient city. What additional evidence is most directly relevant?
steps: Identify the claim: physical city layout.
Look for archaeological plans, excavated features and dated site reports.
Compare the literary account rather than treating it as a measured map.
example.answer: Archaeological/site evidence is directly relevant to the physical-layout claim.

chapters.mistake: Do not treat all ancient dynasties as contemporaneous.

chapters.title: Medieval India: administration, exchange and cultural change

concepts.title: Separate dynasties and institutions
concepts.text: The Delhi Sultanate and Mughal empire are distinct political formations. Identify the ruler, period and region before matching an institution. A military victory, an accession and an administrative reform can have different dates and evidence. Historical labels cover changing arrangements rather than one uniform system for centuries.

concepts.title: Understand administrative terms relationally
concepts.text: In Mughal administration a mansab was a rank within an imperial service structure. A jagir concerned an assigned revenue entitlement in the relevant administrative arrangement; do not automatically translate it into unrestricted private land ownership. Revenue assignment, administrative office and actual agrarian production are related but different categories.

concepts.title: Study cultural processes through specific examples
concepts.text: Bhakti and Sufi traditions included diverse teachers, regions, languages and practices. Avoid presenting them as one identical doctrine. Architecture should be linked to its site, patronage, materials and form. Trade and towns connect production, routes and demand; a coin find alone does not quantify the entire volume of trade.

example.problem: A matching exercise treats mansab, jagir and a peasant’s crop output as identical. How should the categories be separated?
steps: Jagir concerns a specified revenue assignment.
Crop output is production; it is not itself an office or rank.
example.answer: Rank, revenue assignment and production are distinct.

recall: Study cultural processes through specific examples
chapters.mistake: Do not convert every revenue assignment into modern unrestricted land ownership.

chapters.title: Modern India: movements, institutions and causal claims

concepts.title: Organise events and objectives
concepts.text: A chronology should pair each event with its immediate objective, leadership and context. The Revolt of 1857, civil-disobedience mobilisation around the Salt March in 1930, Quit India in 1942 and independence in 1947 are distinct episodes. Do not reduce long political change to a single date or one cause.

concepts.title: Separate law, protest and participation
concepts.text: A movement can challenge a specific law while also articulating broader political goals. Different regions and social groups can participate in different ways. A slogan, a resolution, a legal change and its implementation are separate sources of evidence. Contemporary official accounts and movement participants may describe the same event differently.

concepts.title: Use source comparison in answers
concepts.text: For assertion-reason questions, test each assertion independently and then test whether the reason actually explains it. Temporal sequence alone does not establish causality. Locate named organisations and constitutional changes in their correct period before using them to explain events. A thematic revision table is more useful than an undated list of leaders.

example.problem: Order 1857, the Salt March, Quit India and independence, then state why ordering alone is not a causal explanation.
steps: Explaining causes also requires evidence about mechanisms and context.
example.answer: 1857 → 1930 → 1942 → 1947; timing alone does not prove causation.

chapters.mistake: Do not equate an immediate protest objective with the entire movement.

chapters.title: Indian physical geography: relief, drainage and map reading

concepts.title: Relate landforms to processes
concepts.text: The Himalayas and the peninsular plateau have different geological histories and landform characteristics. Northern plains are associated with extensive river deposits. A map exercise should distinguish mountains, plateaus, plains, coastal belts and islands rather than memorising one undifferentiated list of names.

concepts.title: Follow drainage from source to mouth
concepts.text: A drainage basin is the area contributing runoff to a river system; a watershed separates drainage areas. Many major Himalayan rivers are supported by multiple seasonal sources, while peninsular rivers reflect their own catchment and rainfall conditions. The Narmada and Tapi are important west-flowing peninsular examples. Avoid claiming every peninsular river flows east.

concepts.title: Read the map’s conventions
concepts.text: A scale converts a measured map distance to ground distance under the stated projection and accuracy. A contour joins equal elevation; close contours indicate a steeper local gradient than widely spaced ones on a consistent map. Cardinal direction must be tied to the map orientation. Practice locating features on a blank map before using labels.

example.problem: A map scale is 1:200,000. Two points are 3 cm apart on the map. Find the corresponding ground distance under the scale assumption.
steps: One map cm represents 200,000 cm on the ground.

recall: Follow drainage from source to mouth
chapters.mistake: Map distance and angular coordinates are not the same quantity.

chapters.title: Climate, monsoon and agricultural conditions

concepts.title: Distinguish weather and climate
concepts.text: Weather concerns short-term atmospheric conditions; climate describes their statistical patterns over a stated period. A single hot day does not establish a long-term trend. Temperature, pressure, winds, humidity and precipitation interact, and a regional pattern can differ from a national average.

concepts.title: Explain seasonal rainfall with context
concepts.text: The South Asian monsoon involves seasonal circulation changes, land-sea contrasts and larger atmospheric-oceanic influences. Relief can lift moist air and create differences between windward and leeward conditions. Actual seasonal rainfall varies across regions and years; use dated meteorological evidence for current conditions rather than treating a long-term pattern as a forecast.

concepts.title: Link farming to several constraints
concepts.text: Crop suitability depends on temperature, water, soil, growing period, inputs and management. Kharif and rabi are seasonal classifications in the Indian context, with regional variation. Irrigation changes water access but does not remove every climate or soil constraint. Renewable resources can still be depleted locally if use exceeds regeneration.

example.problem: A station records 100,120,80 and 100 mm over four months. Find the average monthly rainfall and explain whether that alone establishes a climate trend.
steps: Average over the four observations=100 mm.
A trend requires an appropriate longer and comparable time series.
example.answer: 100 mm average; these four values alone do not establish a long-term climate trend.

chapters.mistake: A crop-season label is not a universal planting date for every region.

chapters.title: Indian culture: forms, sites and evidence-based associations

concepts.title: Build associations with more than one clue
concepts.text: For an art form or monument, record region, broad period, tradition, materials and a reliable source. A site can contain structures from different phases. A modern administrative boundary should not automatically be projected onto every historical cultural region.

concepts.title: Distinguish cultural categories
concepts.text: Architecture, sculpture, painting, performing arts, literature and craft traditions overlap but are not interchangeable labels. Stupa, temple and mosque describe different architectural/religious contexts; a named site may require more precise identification. A text’s language, genre and broad historical context help avoid confusing authors and works.

concepts.title: Treat heritage labels as dated claims
concepts.text: A tradition’s continued practice, a legal protection category and an international heritage listing are distinct claims. Current recognition lists should be checked on the responsible authority’s site with the year. This lesson does not claim a current count of monuments, classical languages or heritage inscriptions. Use a source-backed association notebook rather than guessing from a familiar photograph.

example.problem: A flashcard says a monument was built in one day by a ruler who lived centuries later. How should it be checked?
steps: Verify the monument’s location and construction phases.
Compare the ruler’s documented period with those phases.
Replace the claim only when a reliable site/history source supports the association.
example.answer: Use chronology and site evidence together.

recall: Build associations with more than one clue
Treat heritage labels as dated claims
chapters.mistake: Do not infer a current heritage designation from the age of a site.

chapters.title: Constitutional roles, federalism and local institutions

concepts.title: Separate institutional roles
concepts.text: Parliament is the Union legislature, the executive administers within the constitutional framework and courts adjudicate. In a parliamentary system the council of ministers is collectively responsible to the appropriate elected house under the governing provisions. These functions interact; they are not completely isolated compartments.

concepts.title: Read federal distribution carefully
concepts.text: The constitutional distribution of legislative subjects uses Union, State and Concurrent Lists with specified rules and exceptions. Do not infer that the same institution makes every rule at every level. Local-government arrangements have constitutional and state-law details; a local service function should be matched to the competent body and jurisdiction.

concepts.title: Distinguish remedies and policy direction
concepts.text: Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles have different enforceability roles. A political promise, a policy guideline, a statute and a constitutional provision are different kinds of authority. For an article-number or exceptional-powers question, consult the current official text rather than extending a broad summary beyond its conditions.

example.problem: A note says every policy goal is a directly enforceable Fundamental Right. Identify the error.
steps: Distinguish Fundamental Rights from Directive Principles.
Check the particular legal remedy rather than inferring it from the desirability of the goal.
example.answer: Policy direction and judicially enforceable rights are different constitutional categories.

chapters.mistake: A slogan does not establish the institution’s legal competence.

chapters.title: Human biology: transport, exchange and regulation

concepts.title: Follow transport and exchange
concepts.text: Blood transports substances around the body. Red blood cells and haemoglobin are central to oxygen transport; the heart pumps blood through circulation. Gas exchange occurs across specialised respiratory surfaces, while breathing moves air. Breathing and cellular respiration are related but different processes.

concepts.title: Separate digestion and absorption
concepts.text: Digestion breaks food into absorbable forms through mechanical and chemical processes. Absorption transfers digested substances across the intestinal surface. Enzymes have specific actions and conditions; a body organ is not identified merely by its location near food passage. Nutrient deficiency questions require the specific nutrient and established biological role.

concepts.title: Understand coordination
concepts.text: Nervous signalling and hormonal regulation coordinate functions through different mechanisms. Homeostasis concerns controlled internal conditions, not perfect invariance. Pathogens and vectors are different: a vector can carry a disease-causing agent without being the same organism as that agent. These are general-science essentials, not personal medical advice.

example.problem: A diagram labels movement of air as cellular respiration and absorption as digestion. Correct the distinctions.
steps: Ventilation/breathing moves air; gas exchange transfers gases.
Cellular respiration releases/transfers usable energy from fuels in cells.
Digestion breaks food down; absorption transfers products across a surface.
example.answer: Name the process by what it does, not by a nearby organ.

chapters.mistake: A disease vector and its pathogen are not the same category.

chapters.title: Tier-II maths: descriptive statistics and elementary probability

concepts.title: Choose the right summary
concepts.text: Mean uses all values; median uses ordered position; mode identifies the most frequent value and can be nonunique. To combine groups, reconstruct totals rather than average means without weights. Use a specified finite-sample convention for quartiles and related partition values.

concepts.title: Calculate squared spread consistently
concepts.text: For a fully specified population, variance is the mean squared deviation and SD its nonnegative square root. For sample estimation the usual unbiased variance divides by n−1. State which is intended. Adding a constant preserves spread; multiplying by b scales SD by |b|.

concepts.title: Define the experiment before counting
concepts.text: Elementary probability requires a sample space, events and justified probabilities. Fairness and independence are assumptions, not automatic consequences of using a coin or die. For a conditioned event, restrict the denominator to the given information. Complement and union laws help avoid double counting.

example.problem: For the full population {2,2,4,8}, find mean, median and mode.
steps: Total=16 over four observations gives mean 4.
Ordered middle values are 2 and 4, so median 3.

chapters.mistake: Do not label an arbitrary dataset population or sample without reading the question.

chapters.title: Visual reasoning: rotations, reflections and folded paper

concepts.title: Declare the transformation and axis
concepts.text: A vertical mirror reverses horizontal direction; a horizontal mirror reverses vertical direction. A quarter-turn rotation changes direction without the same handedness reversal as a reflection. Read the operation order and viewpoint; doing reflection then rotation need not equal rotation then reflection.

concepts.title: Track labelled elements rather than resemblance
concepts.text: Use the marked corner, dot, arrowhead or line segment as an anchor. Check every component of a figure before choosing an option. For a matrix, identify a consistent row/column relation supported by the supplied cells; an invented rule that fits only one cell is insufficient.

concepts.title: Unfold in reverse order
concepts.text: A hole punched through folded layers is reflected across each fold when unfolded. Holes on a fold may coincide; holes away from all fold lines yield distinct reflected locations under the described simple folds. The original diagrams below are accessible visual drills, not authenticated SSC figures or a comprehensive visual-reasoning bank.

example.problem: An east-pointing arrow is reflected across a vertical mirror and then rotated clockwise by 90°. Find its final direction.
steps: The vertical mirror changes east to west.
Clockwise rotation from west gives north.
Applying the operations in reverse order need not give the same answer.

recall: Track labelled elements rather than resemblance
chapters.mistake: Keep the transformation order fixed.

questions.stem: English drill (idioms): Choose the standard sentence.
options: She suggested me a new approach to do it yesterday is.
She did suggested a new approach.
questions.explanation: Suggested directly introduces the proposed approach in this sentence.

questions.stem: English drill (idioms): To call off an event means to:
options: Always postpone it for one day
questions.explanation: Call off means cancel.

questions.stem: English drill (idioms): Under the weather in an everyday idiom commonly means:
questions.explanation: The idiom commonly describes feeling ill or unwell.

questions.stem: English drill (idioms): Choose the less redundant expression.
options: Repeat again once more the instruction.
Repeat back again once more the instruction.
questions.explanation: Repeat already conveys doing/saying it again; the shortest option avoids redundant repetition.

questions.stem: English drill (reading): Original passage: A school planted trees beside one classroom. That room was cooler the following summer, but its roof was also replaced. Which is established?
options: The room was cooler after both changes
questions.explanation: The observation does not isolate which concurrent change caused the difference.

questions.stem: English drill (reading): Original passage: A survey of 50 volunteers found 30 preferred evening classes. No random sample was drawn. Which statement follows directly?
questions.explanation: The reported count concerns the volunteers, not an established representative population estimate.

questions.stem: English drill (reading): Original passage: A library lends reference books for seven days. Rare manuscripts are excluded. Can every library item be borrowed for seven days?
options: No; the passage expressly excludes rare manuscripts
The passage says all items are manuscripts
questions.explanation: The exception defeats the universal claim.

questions.stem: English drill (reading): Order: P:Finally, she checked the result. Q:First, she read the problem. R:Then, she chose a method.
questions.explanation: The explicit sequence is first Q, then R, finally P.

questions.stem: English drill (reading): Choose the cause connector: The road was flooded; ___, the bus was delayed.
questions.explanation: Therefore links the delay as a consequence of the flooding.

questions.stem: English drill (reading): Original passage: Some participants improved their score. No score decreased. Which is supported?
options: At least one score improved and none decreased
questions.explanation: Some establishes a nonempty improved group; the rest need not have improved.

questions.stem: Which device primarily produces printed output?
questions.explanation: A printer produces physical output.

questions.stem: Which unit executes program instructions?
questions.explanation: The CPU executes instructions in the standard computer model.

questions.stem: A 16-bit quantity occupies how many 8-bit bytes?
questions.explanation: 16/8=2 bytes.

questions.stem: An SSD is normally used for:
questions.explanation: An SSD retains stored data without continuous power in normal operation.

questions.stem: A folder primarily helps organise:
questions.explanation: Folders organise filesystem entries.

questions.stem: A device driver primarily enables the operating system to:
options: Make an unsaved file persistent automatically
questions.explanation: Drivers provide device-specific communication/control support.

questions.stem: In common Windows desktop editing, Ctrl+A usually means:
questions.explanation: Ctrl+A commonly selects all applicable content.

questions.stem: Ctrl+P commonly opens:
questions.explanation: Ctrl+P is a common print shortcut.

questions.stem: A slide animation commonly applies to:
questions.explanation: Animations act on slide objects; transitions act between slides.

questions.stem: A word-processing header is commonly located:
options: Only in a spreadsheet formula bar
In the top page margin area
questions.explanation: Headers are page elements typically placed in the top margin area.

questions.stem: To preserve an original while editing a separate working copy, use:
questions.explanation: A separate file allows independent changes while preserving the original.

questions.stem: An exported PDF should be opened to check:
questions.explanation: Inspect the output itself; an extension alone does not prove correct rendering.

questions.stem: Copy =A1+1 from B1 to B2. The relative-reference result is:
questions.explanation: Moving down one row shifts A1 to A2.

questions.stem: Which range includes A1, A2, A3, A4?
questions.explanation: Colon notation denotes the inclusive cell range.

questions.stem: If A1=5 and A2=7, =SUM(A1:A2)*2 gives:
The formula =(8+4)/3 evaluates to:
questions.explanation: Parentheses give 12, then divide by 3.

questions.stem: Which reference locks the row but permits the column to shift?
questions.explanation: The dollar sign before 1 fixes the row.

questions.stem: A cell containing 0.125 displayed as a percentage shows:
questions.explanation: Percentage format displays the stored fraction multiplied by 100.

questions.stem: Which email field normally shows additional copied recipients to others?
questions.explanation: CC recipients are normally visible in the recipient information.

questions.stem: A search engine and browser are:
options: Different roles even if used together
Always the same program and service
questions.explanation: A browser displays web resources; a search engine provides indexed retrieval.

questions.stem: Downloading a file means transferring it:
options: From a remote service to the local device
questions.explanation: Download is inbound transfer to the local device in the stated context.

questions.stem: A self-spreading malware program across networks is commonly described as a:
questions.explanation: A worm can replicate/spread across systems; the term is distinct from ordinary application components.

questions.stem: A useful protection against losing files to device failure is:
questions.explanation: An independent backup can preserve recoverable copies when the primary device fails.

questions.stem: Before Reply All, you should inspect:
questions.explanation: Reply All can send content to multiple original recipients, so inspect who receives it.
